SECTION 1
What Are AI Logs?

When you use Claude Code, every conversation you have with Claude is automatically saved to your computer as a .jsonl file (JSON Lines format). Each line in the file is a record of one message — your prompt, Claude's response, or a tool action Claude took on your behalf.

These log files are your evidence for C1 — AI Workflow. They show your tutor:

    →
    What you asked Claude to do — your prompts across design, coding, testing, and deployment phases.
    →
    What Claude produced — the code, explanations, or suggestions it generated.
    →
    How your prompting evolved — whether you refined prompts, pushed back on Claude's output, or changed direction.

🤖 You do not need to manually write these logs — Claude Code creates them automatically. Your job is to copy them into your project repository before submitting.
SECTION 2
Where to Find Your Logs

Claude Code stores your conversation logs as .jsonl files in a hidden folder on your computer. The location depends on your operating system.
# Windows
C:\Users\<your-username>\.claude\projects\<code-folder>\

# macOS / Linux
~/.claude/projects/

Inside the projects/ folder, each Claude Code project has its own subfolder. Inside that folder you will find .jsonl files — one file per conversation session.
Example log folder structure
~/.claude/projects/ └── your-project-id/ ├── 2024-11-01T09-32-11.jsonl # session on 1 Nov — design phase ├── 2024-11-04T14-08-55.jsonl # session on 4 Nov — coding backend ├── 2024-11-08T10-22-30.jsonl # session on 8 Nov — debugging └── 2024-11-12T16-45-02.jsonl # session on 12 Nov — testing
⚠️ On Windows, folders starting with a dot (like .claude) may be hidden by default. To see it, open File Explorer, click View → Show → Hidden items, then navigate to C:\Users\<your-username>\.claude\projects\.
SECTION 3
Backup Your Logs

Before you commit your code, copy any new .jsonl files from your Claude project log folder into your repository under ai/<your-name>/ai-logs/. This is your submission folder for C1.
Where to copy them
Your repository
your-project/ └── ai/ └── <your-name>/ └── ai-logs/ ├── 2024-11-01T09-32-11.jsonl ├── 2024-11-04T14-08-55.jsonl ├── 2024-11-08T10-22-30.jsonl └── 2024-11-12T16-45-02.jsonl
Step-by-step

    1
    Open your Claude log folder

    Navigate to ~/.claude/projects/<your-project-id>/ on macOS, or C:\Users\<your-username>\.claude\projects\<code-folder>\ on Windows.
    2
    Copy any new .jsonl files

    Identify any .jsonl files you haven't copied yet. Copy them — don't move them. The originals stay in the Claude folder.
    3
    Paste into your repository

    Paste the files into ai/<your-name>/ai-logs/ inside your project repository.
    4
    Commit and push

    Include the log files in your next commit. Use a clear message like add ai logs for week 3.

✅ Don't wait until the final submission to copy your logs. Back them up regularly — after each working session is ideal. This also shows your tutor that you used AI throughout the project, not just at the end.
SECTION 4
Starting a New Chat Without Losing Progress

Claude Code conversations have a context limit. When a chat gets very long — or when you start working on a different part of the project — Claude may lose track of earlier decisions. Starting a new chat solves this, but you don't want to lose the context of where you left off.

The solution is a handoff summary: ask Claude to write a summary of the current session before you close it, then paste that summary into your next chat to instantly pick up where you left off.
Step 1 — Generate a handoff summary

At the end of your current session, type the following prompt into Claude Code:
Prompt to Claude — end of session Please write a handoff summary for this session. Include:
- What we were working on and the current state
- Key decisions made and the reasoning behind them
- Files created or modified
- What still needs to be done
- Any known issues or things to watch out for

Claude will produce a structured summary. Copy it and save it — paste it into a note, a text file, or directly into your next chat.
Example handoff summary (Claude's output)

Current state: We built the user authentication flow — registration and login endpoints are complete and tested. JWT tokens are issued on login and verified via middleware.

Key decisions: Used bcrypt with 10 salt rounds for password hashing. Chose short-lived access tokens (15 min) with refresh token logic to be added next.

Files modified: backend/src/routes/auth.js, backend/src/middleware/auth.js, backend/src/models/User.js

Still to do: Refresh token endpoint, protected route testing, frontend login form integration.

Watch out for: The JWT_SECRET env variable must be set in Render before deploying — deployment will fail without it.
Step 2 — Start a new chat with the handoff summary

Open a new Claude Code chat and begin with the following prompt, pasting your summary where indicated:
Prompt to Claude — start of new session I'm continuing work on my full stack project. Here is a summary of where we left off:

[paste your handoff summary here]

Let's continue from here. Today I want to work on [describe your goal for this session].

Claude will read the summary and have the full context it needs to continue helping you effectively — without you needing to re-explain everything.
✅ A good handoff summary is also useful for your own reflection. Keep a copy in a notes/ folder or your personal notes app — it helps you write your ai-reflection.md at the end of the project.
⚠️ Remember to back up your logs before starting a new chat. Each chat session creates a new .jsonl file — copy the completed session's file into ai/<your-name>/ai-logs/ before you close it.
